objectives: Distinguish operational vs embodied carbon + the AIA / RIBA 2030 commitments (Architecture 2030, Mazria).
Survey certification systems — LEED, BREEAM, WELL, Living Building Challenge, Passivhaus.
Explore biophilic design (Kellert), biomimicry (Benyus + Pearce's Eastgate), circular economy + cradle-to-cradle (McDonough + Braungart).

slides.title: Operational + embodied carbon + the 2030 commitments
slides.body:
**Buildings account for ~40% of global CO₂ emissions** (UN Environment 2020; IEA tracking). Two components:
- **Operational carbon (~28% of global)**: emissions from energy used during the building's lifetime — heating, cooling, lighting, equipment. Driven by envelope efficiency + system efficiency + grid carbon intensity.
- **Embodied carbon (~11% of global)**: emissions released to manufacture + transport + construct + maintain + dispose of building materials. Cement, steel, aluminum dominate; lesson 3 covers material-level coefficients.

Historically the industry focused on operational carbon (energy codes, ASHRAE 90.1, LEED EAc1, ENERGY STAR). As grids decarbonize + new buildings reach Passivhaus-grade envelope performance, operational carbon shrinks toward zero — and **embodied carbon increasingly dominates** the lifetime emissions of new construction. Today's high-performance buildings have ~50-70% of their *lifetime* carbon already emitted by the time they open.

**Architecture 2030 + Edward Mazria**:
- **Edward Mazria** — American architect (Albuquerque, NM); his 2006 *Architecture 2030 Challenge* reframed the building sector as a primary climate actor.
- Founded **Architecture 2030** (non-profit) — analyzed building-sector emissions globally + set incremental carbon targets.
- **2030 Challenge**: all new buildings + major renovations to use 70% less fossil-fuel energy than the regional average for that building type — escalating to **carbon neutral by 2030**. Originally focused on operational; expanded in 2018 to include embodied carbon.
- **CARE Tool, AIA 2030 Design Data Exchange (DDX)** for tracking firm portfolio progress.
- Adopted as policy by AIA, ASHRAE, US Conference of Mayors, USGBC, RIBA, Public Architecture, NYC + Boston + Toronto.

**AIA 2030 Commitment**:
- **American Institute of Architects** initiative (~2009-); signatory firms commit to AIA 2030 carbon-reduction targets.
- **DDX (Design Data Exchange)**: firms report energy + carbon performance of every project annually; aggregated portfolio data tracks progress against 2030 goals.
- As of 2024, ~1500+ firms participate; portfolio averages ~50% energy reduction below baseline (still short of 100% by 2030 target).

**RIBA 2030 Climate Challenge**:
- **Royal Institute of British Architects** sister commitment; explicit operational AND embodied carbon targets:
  - 2025: operational ≤ 55 kWh/m²·yr (offices ≤ 75), embodied ≤ 800 kg CO₂e/m².
  - 2030: operational ≤ 35 kWh/m²·yr (offices ≤ 50), embodied ≤ 625 kg CO₂e/m² (offices), with potable water + biodiversity + circularity also tracked.
- More aggressive + more comprehensive than the AIA equivalent.

**LETI (London Energy Transformation Initiative)**:
- UK industry coalition (2017-) — *Climate Emergency Design Guide*. Building-typology-specific operational + embodied targets aligned with UK net-zero 2050.

**Embodied-carbon tools + databases** (recapping lesson 3):
- **Hammond + Jones ICE (Inventory of Carbon + Energy)** — University of Bath; open coefficient database.
- **EC3 (Embodied Carbon in Construction Calculator)** — Carbon Leadership Forum + Building Transparency; product-level EPDs for procurement.
- **Tally** (Revit plug-in), **OneClickLCA**, **Athena Impact Estimator**, **Cove.tool** carbon modules.
- **EN 15978** (European building LCA standard), **ISO 14040/14044** (general LCA).
- **EPDs (Environmental Product Declarations)**: standardized, third-party-verified material carbon disclosures.

**Net-zero + carbon-positive + carbon-negative**:
- **Net-zero operational**: annual energy use balanced by on-site or contracted renewables. Definitions: net-zero site, source, energy, cost.
- **Net-zero embodied**: cradle-to-grave + offsets = 0. Very aggressive; depends heavily on biogenic carbon sequestration + offsets.
- **Net-zero whole-life**: operational + embodied + maintenance + demolition net zero — the most rigorous target.
- **Carbon-positive** buildings produce more energy than they consume; **carbon-negative** materials store more CO₂ than they release.
- Examples: PowerHouse projects in Norway (Snøhetta + Skanska); ILFI Living Building Challenge projects.

**Policy levers**:
- **EU EPBD recast 2024**: all new buildings ZEB (Zero Emission Building) by 2030; all existing by 2050.
- **US IRA 2022** funding for green steel + cement + GeoSync + retrofit.
- **Buy Clean California (2017) + Buy Clean federal (2022 EO)**: low-carbon material procurement for state-funded buildings.
- **Local Law 97 (NYC 2019)**: ~50000 buildings >25000 ft² subject to emissions caps, fines starting 2024.

slides.title: Certification systems: LEED, BREEAM, WELL, Living Building Challenge, Passivhaus
slides.body:
Certification systems translate sustainability ambition into measurable + comparable performance — and into market signals (rents, sales premiums, tenant preferences). Five dominate.

**LEED (Leadership in Energy + Environmental Design) — USGBC 1998**:
- US Green Building Council (founded 1993) launched LEED v1.0 in 1998. Now **LEED v4.1** (2019) + LEED v5 (in development 2024-25).
- Most-used green building rating system globally (>110000 certified projects across 180+ countries).
- **Categories**: Location + Transportation, Sustainable Sites, Water Efficiency, Energy + Atmosphere (largest weight, ~30% of points), Materials + Resources, Indoor Environmental Quality, Innovation, Regional Priority.
- **Certification levels**: Certified (40-49 pts), Silver (50-59), Gold (60-79), Platinum (80+). Maximum 110 points.
- **Rating systems by use**: LEED BD+C (Building Design + Construction), ID+C (Interior), O+M (Existing Buildings), ND (Neighborhood Development), Homes, Cities + Communities.
- v4 added stronger emphasis on integrative process + life-cycle thinking + material disclosure (EPDs, HPDs Health Product Declarations).
- Critique: prescriptive + checklist-driven; rewards intent more than performance (gap between design + operational data).

**BREEAM (Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method) — UK 1990**:
- World's longest-running green building certification — BRE 1990. The original.
- Categories: Management, Health + Wellbeing, Energy, Transport, Water, Materials, Waste, Land Use + Ecology, Pollution, Innovation.
- **Ratings**: Pass, Good, Very Good, Excellent, Outstanding.
- Stronger in UK + Europe + the Middle East; ~600000+ certified projects.
- Generally regarded as more rigorous on energy performance + life-cycle than LEED.

**WELL Building Standard — IWBI 2014**:
- International WELL Building Institute (Delos founder, Paul Scialla); v2 released 2018.
- **Focus**: human health + wellbeing — air, water, nourishment, light, movement, thermal comfort, sound, materials, mind, community.
- **Performance-verified** (post-occupancy testing of air, water, light, etc.), not just design-credit checklist.
- Aligned with research from Harvard T.H. Chan School (Joseph Allen, *Healthy Buildings*), Center for Active Design.
- Companion to LEED + Passivhaus + Living Building Challenge — focused on the *occupant* rather than the *planet*.
- Adopted by corporate offices, healthcare, schools, residential.

**Living Building Challenge (LBC) — ILFI (International Living Future Institute) 2006**:
- Jason F. McLennan (Cascadia GBC). Founded as the most rigorous green building certification in existence.
- **Seven petals**: Place, Water, Energy, Health + Happiness, Materials, Equity, Beauty.
- Each petal contains *imperatives* (mandatory requirements) — e.g., **Net Positive Energy** (105% of annual energy from on-site renewables), **Net Positive Water** (closed-loop, no municipal water + sewage), **Materials Red List** (declares + avoids 23+ classes of toxic materials), **Equitable Investment**, **Beauty + Spirit** (the building must inspire).
- Performance verified after **12 months of operation** — among the strictest in the world.
- **Petal Certification** (achieve 3+ petals); **Living Certification** (all 7).
- Less than 200 fully certified Living Buildings (vs 110k+ LEED) — by design difficult; sets the practice frontier. Examples: Bullitt Center Seattle (Miller Hull 2013), Frick Environmental Center Pittsburgh.

**Passivhaus (Wolfgang Feist + Bo Adamson 1991)** — see lesson 5. Performance-based; 50000+ certified buildings worldwide; the foundational low-energy building performance benchmark.

**Other notable systems**:
- **DGNB** (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Nachhaltiges Bauen, Germany 2007): German + global; rigorous LCA-based.
- **Green Star** (Australia 2003).
- **HQE** (Haute Qualité Environnementale, France).
- **CASBEE** (Comprehensive Assessment System for Built Environment Efficiency, Japan).
- **EDGE** (IFC/World Bank, emerging markets).
- **Fitwel** (CDC + GSA, lighter-touch health-focused).
- **Energy Star** (US EPA, performance-rated).
- **Net Zero Energy Certification (NZEC, ILFI)**.

**Critique + future**:
- Pre-certification vs operational gap: certified buildings often perform 20-50% worse than design predictions (NREL studies). LEED + WELL increasingly require post-occupancy verification.
- Greenwashing risk: certification used as marketing without genuine performance change.
- **The next decade**: convergence toward whole-life carbon accounting (operational + embodied), occupant health + equity, climate resilience, and continuous performance disclosure (energy + water + air + occupant outcome dashboards).

slides.title: Biophilic + biomimicry + cradle-to-cradle + circular economy
slides.body:
Sustainability is more than carbon. Three complementary frameworks reshape what *good* architecture means: **biophilic design** (humans need nature in their built environment), **biomimicry** (design lessons from nature's solutions), and **cradle-to-cradle + circular economy** (close the materials loop).

**Biophilic design — Stephen Kellert**:
- **Stephen R. Kellert** (1943-2016, Yale F&ES). *The Biophilia Hypothesis* (1993, with E.O. Wilson) + *Biophilic Design* (2008, with Heerwagen + Mador) + *The Practice of Biophilic Design* (2015).
- Builds on E. O. Wilson's 1984 *Biophilia* — the hypothesis that humans have an innate affinity for nature shaped by evolutionary history.
- **14 patterns of biophilic design** (Terrapin Bright Green 2014, with Kellert + William Browning): 1. Visual connection with nature; 2. Non-visual connection (sound, smell, touch); 3. Non-rhythmic sensory stimuli; 4. Thermal + airflow variability; 5. Presence of water; 6. Dynamic + diffuse light; 7. Connection with natural systems; 8. Biomorphic forms; 9. Material connection with nature; 10. Complexity + order; 11. Prospect + refuge; 12. Mystery; 13. Risk + peril; 14. Awe.
- **Health + productivity evidence**: hospital views of nature reduce recovery time (Roger Ulrich 1984 *Science* hospital study); office views + plants reduce stress + improve cognitive performance (Joseph Allen Harvard COGfx studies, William Browning + Terrapin Bright Green's *The Economics of Biophilia*).
- **Examples**: Khoo Teck Puat Hospital Singapore (CPG Consultants), Amazon Spheres Seattle (NBBJ), Bullitt Center Seattle, Apple Park courtyard, Singapore's Park Royal on Pickering (WOHA).
- Integration: WELL + LBC reward biophilic patterns; sometimes treated as the *qualitative* complement to LEED's *quantitative*.

**Biomimicry — Janine Benyus**:
- **Janine Benyus** — *Biomimicry: Innovation Inspired by Nature* (1997). Founded the **Biomimicry Institute** (2006) + **Biomimicry 3.8** (consultancy).
- **Principle**: nature has run a 3.8-billion-year R&D process; its successful designs are field-tested + energy-efficient + waste-free + locally adapted. Architects + engineers + product designers can ask: *what would nature do here?*
- **Levels of biomimicry**: form (mimic shape), process (mimic mechanism), ecosystem (mimic systems-level behavior).
- **Architecture examples**:
  - **Mick Pearce — Eastgate Centre Harare, Zimbabwe (1996)**: office + retail building inspired by **termite mounds** (Macrotermes michaelseni) which maintain a near-constant 30°C interior despite outside swings of 1.5° to 40°C. Pearce + Arup engineers designed Eastgate with night-flushed thermal mass + passive ventilation through stacks — no conventional air-conditioning. Uses ~10% of the energy of a comparable conventional building. **The canonical biomimetic building**.
  - **Pearce's CH2 Melbourne** (2006) extends the strategy.
  - **Beijing Olympic 'Water Cube'** (PTW Architects + Arup 2008): ETFE-clad steel structure with bubble-pattern facade derived from foam geometry (Weaire-Phelan structure).
  - **Esplanade Theatres Singapore** (DP + Michael Wilford 2002): durian-fruit-inspired thermal shading.
  - **30 St Mary Axe London 'Gherkin'** (Foster + Partners 2003): sea-sponge-inspired diagrid + ventilation pattern.
- **AskNature.org** — Biomimicry Institute database of biological strategies for engineering + design problems.

**Cradle-to-Cradle — William McDonough + Michael Braungart (2002)**:
- **William McDonough** — American architect (1996 *Hannover Principles* with German chemist Braungart for Expo 2000); founder McDonough Innovation, McDonough + Partners.
- **Michael Braungart** — German chemist (EPEA Hamburg, founder of green chemistry research).
- *Cradle to Cradle: Remaking the Way We Make Things* (2002) — argues against *cradle-to-grave* (linear extract → make → use → landfill) toward closed-loop *cradle-to-cradle* (materials cycle indefinitely as either *biological nutrients* or *technical nutrients*).
- **Three principles**: waste = food; use current solar income; celebrate diversity.
- **C2C Certified** (Cradle to Cradle Products Innovation Institute, 2010-): product certification across material health, material reutilization, renewable energy, water stewardship, social fairness. Bronze → Silver → Gold → Platinum.
- Influence: shifted material thinking from *reduce harm* to *positively beneficial*. Influences ILFI Materials Red List + EU circular-economy policy + EPEA-style chemical reformulation.
- Critiques: hard to scale; sometimes accused of utopianism; effectively delivered through stepwise improvements at major firms (Herman Miller, Steelcase, Shaw Industries).

**Circular economy**:
- **Ellen MacArthur Foundation** (2010-) — global circular-economy advocacy; standard reference framework.
- **Five circular strategies**: refuse, reduce, reuse, repair, recycle (R-ladder, variously 5R-9R).
- **Adaptive reuse**: renovate existing buildings rather than demolish + rebuild. The lowest-carbon project (embodied carbon already paid). Tate Modern (Bankside Power Station → Herzog & de Meuron 2000), High Line (Diller Scofidio + Renfro 2009), Battersea Power Station, Cement Park (Bofill).
- **Design for disassembly (DfD)**: design buildings + components so they can be taken apart + reused or recycled. Mechanical connections > glued; standardized modules > custom; material passports recording every component's identity + history.
- **Material passport**: digital ledger of every material in a building — composition, location, condition, end-of-life options. Madaster (Netherlands), BAMB (Buildings As Material Banks, EU project).
- **Modular + relocatable buildings**: WikiHouse, AbleNook, Kasita; designed to be disassembled + relocated.

**Integration in practice**: leading firms (Mithun, KieranTimberlake, Lake|Flato, WOHA, Snøhetta, Foster + Partners, ZGF) increasingly integrate biophilic + biomimetic + cradle-to-cradle + circular thinking into the design process from concept onward — not as a checklist add-on but as a generative framework. The Living Building Challenge's seven petals + the AIA Framework for Design Excellence make this explicit.

Climate change + biodiversity collapse + resource scarcity are reframing architecture from *neutral service* to *active regenerator*. The discipline is moving from *less bad* to *net positive* — buildings that produce more energy + clean more water + sequester more carbon + host more biodiversity than they consume + harm + emit + displace. The frontier is in lesson 8.

question.question: Whole-life carbon accounting for a new office
question.goal: A 5000 m² office is being designed. Estimate operational + embodied carbon over a 60-year life + identify the highest-leverage interventions.

steps.prompt: Operational carbon: if energy-use intensity (EUI) is 80 kWh/m²·yr + grid carbon intensity is 0.3 kg CO₂/kWh, what is annual + 60-year operational carbon per m²?
steps.reveal: Annual operational carbon: **80 kWh/m²·yr × 0.3 kg CO₂/kWh = 24 kg CO₂e/m²·yr**. **60-year cumulative: 1440 kg CO₂e/m²**. Note this assumes constant grid intensity; with grid decarbonization the cumulative is much lower — IEA + IPCC trajectories see major-economy grids at 0.05-0.1 kg/kWh by 2040-2050.

steps.prompt: Embodied carbon: typical new office construction is ~400-600 kg CO₂e/m² (Architecture 2030 + RIBA 2030 benchmarks for offices). With reductions (mass timber + low-carbon concrete + recycled steel), what range becomes achievable?

acceptedAnswers: typical baseline 400 to 600 kg CO₂e/m²; with mass timber + low-carbon concrete + recycled steel + reduced cladding 200 to 350 kg/m²; RIBA 2030 target ≤ 625 kg for offices and aspirational targets ≤ 300 kg

steps.reveal: **Typical baseline office embodied carbon**: 400-600 kg CO₂e/m² cradle-to-gate (RIBA 2030 + Architecture 2030 benchmarks). **With low-carbon strategies** — mass timber structure (lesson 3), low-clinker / SCM concrete, recycled-steel mini-mill, lighter envelope, biogenic insulation — achievable: **200-350 kg CO₂e/m²**. **Aspirational** (Living Building Challenge + leading projects): 100-200 kg/m². RIBA 2030 *office target* ≤ 625 kg/m² (already met by many low-carbon designs); RIBA 2030 *aspirational* ≤ 300.

steps.prompt: Compare cumulative operational (60-year, decarbonizing grid) + embodied. Which dominates for a high-performance + grid-decarbonizing future + what does this imply for design priorities?

acceptedAnswers: with grid decarbonization operational cumulative drops to perhaps 600 to 900 kg over 60 years while embodied carbon (200 to 600 kg) is upfront and irreversible — so embodied carbon becomes equal-to or larger-than lifetime operational and material choices dominate design priority

steps.reveal: With a **decarbonizing grid** (intensity dropping from 0.3 → 0.05 kg/kWh by mid-century), cumulative 60-year operational carbon for a Passivhaus-grade envelope might be **~600-900 kg CO₂e/m²**. **Embodied carbon (200-600 kg/m²) is now equal-to or larger-than cumulative operational** — and is **paid upfront + irreversible** (a tonne of CO₂ emitted today affects the climate for centuries, regardless of future operational reductions). **Implication**: in high-performance new construction, embodied carbon now dominates the design decision — and material choice (lesson 3) + reuse + structural efficiency are the highest-leverage interventions.

steps.prompt: What additional considerations from biophilic + biomimicry + cradle-to-cradle reshape the project beyond carbon?

acceptedAnswers: biophilic design improves occupant health + productivity; biomimicry inspires passive systems like Pearce's termite-mound Eastgate; cradle-to-cradle + circular economy targets design for disassembly + material passports + adaptive reuse — together making the building a net-positive participant in its ecosystem rather than just a less-bad consumer

steps.reveal: **Biophilic design** (Kellert): incorporate nature views + natural light + materials + water → improved occupant health + productivity + cognitive performance (Harvard COGfx, Browning *Economics of Biophilia*). **Biomimicry** (Benyus + AskNature; Pearce's Eastgate termite-mound ventilation): inspire passive systems that achieve high performance with low energy. **Cradle-to-Cradle + circular economy** (McDonough + Braungart; Ellen MacArthur Foundation): design for disassembly, material passports (Madaster, BAMB), low-toxicity material choices, biological + technical nutrient cycles. Together these reframe the project from *less harmful* to *net positive* — a building that produces more energy + cleaner water + more biodiversity + better health outcomes than it consumes or displaces.

question.question: Why is Mick Pearce's Eastgate Centre (Harare, Zimbabwe, 1996) the canonical biomimetic building?
options: It looks like a termite mound on the outside.

Pearce + Arup engineers studied the passive ventilation + thermal regulation of **termite mounds** (Macrotermes michaelseni in southern Africa) which maintain a near-constant 30 °C interior despite outdoor swings from 1.5 °C to 40 °C — using stack-driven ventilation through a complex internal duct network + the mound's massive thermal mass. They translated this strategy into the building's structure: **massive thermal mass** (the building's concrete) cools at night via outside-air flushing through low-level vents, stores 'coolth' through the day, and is exhausted through chimneys that drive stack ventilation. **No conventional HVAC** — only fans + dampers. **Energy use ~10% of a comparable conventional Harare office building.** It demonstrates Janine Benyus's *Biomimicry* (1997) thesis at full architectural scale: nature's 3.8-billion-year R&D process has solved many of the problems we re-invent expensively. Eastgate launched a generation of biomimetic + passive-design experiments (PTW Water Cube 2008, Foster's Gherkin, Pearce's CH2 Melbourne 2006).
It was the first building made of cob.
question.explanation: Eastgate Centre (Pearce + Arup, Harare 1996) translated termite-mound passive ventilation + thermal regulation into a working office building. Massive thermal mass, night-flush cooling, stack-driven exhaust — no conventional HVAC, ~10% of conventional Harare office energy. The canonical biomimetic building; demonstrates Benyus's *Biomimicry* (1997) thesis at full architectural scale + launched a generation of biomimetic + passive designs (Water Cube 2008, Gherkin, CH2 Melbourne 2006).

slides.workedSolution: Eastgate Centre (Pearce + Arup, Harare 1996) — biomimetic passive ventilation from termite mounds: massive thermal mass + night-flush cooling + stack-driven exhaust. No conventional HVAC; ~10% energy use of comparable conventional building. Canonical demonstration of Benyus's *Biomimicry* (1997) at full architectural scale; launched biomimetic + passive design generation.

question.question: Set carbon + certification targets for a 10000 m² university project
question.prompt: You are the architect for a new 10000 m² engineering building at a public university with stated commitments to AIA 2030 + carbon neutrality by 2040. Develop a sustainability framework that addresses: (a) operational carbon target (EUI + grid + on-site PV); (b) embodied carbon target using Hammond + Jones ICE + EC3 + the RIBA 2030 benchmarks; (c) which certification(s) — LEED Platinum, Passivhaus, Living Building Challenge petal, WELL — make sense for this project + why; (d) biophilic + biomimetic moves; (e) cradle-to-cradle / DfD / adaptive-reuse considerations. Reference Mazria, McDonough + Braungart, Benyus, Pearce, Kellert as appropriate.

question.question: An office building uses 80 kWh/m²·yr in a grid with carbon intensity 0.30 kg CO₂/kWh. What is the annual operational carbon, in kg CO₂e per m²?
question.hint: EUI × grid intensity = operational carbon per m² per year.

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, explain why embodied carbon is becoming the dominant consideration in new construction — and why this elevates lesson-3 material choices to first-order design decisions.
question.rubric: Mentions: historically, operational carbon (heating + cooling + lighting + plug loads) dominated building lifetime emissions, and codes (ASHRAE 90.1, IECC, Title 24, LEED EAc1, ENERGY STAR) + the Passivhaus standard (Feist 1991) drove operational carbon toward zero. Grids are also decarbonizing (IEA + IPCC trajectories from ~0.3 kg/kWh today to ~0.05 by 2050). As both effects compound, the cumulative 60-year operational carbon of a high-performance new building drops to ~600-900 kg CO₂e/m² — comparable to or less than its **embodied carbon** (typically 400-600 kg CO₂e/m² for offices, up to 1000+ for high-end towers). Embodied carbon is **paid upfront + irreversible** + concentrated in concrete + steel + aluminum + glass (cement alone is ~8% of global CO₂). Architecture 2030 (Mazria 2006), AIA 2030 Commitment, RIBA 2030, LETI all now track embodied + operational. Material choice — substituting mass timber for concrete or steel (lesson 3), specifying recycled-EAF steel, low-clinker concrete, biogenic insulation — becomes a first-order design decision. EC3 + Hammond + Jones ICE + EPDs make it tractable. The architect's structural + envelope + finish material choices now matter more for the building's lifetime carbon than the HVAC system did a generation ago.
